rationale: Start with a broad scouting gradient at moderate temperature to elute all 10 compounds if possible while mapping the full elution window and any critical pairs. This should reveal whether retention is compressed, truncated, or overly long, guiding narrower-window and slope adjustments next.

All pairs are already fully resolved, so the only available gain is reducing analysis time. Keep the same broad window and temperature and shorten the gradient one step to see how much t_last falls before any pair approaches the 1.5 resolution threshold.

The current method is close to the 10 min target and the limiting pair is still just above the 1.5 threshold, so another small reduction in gradient time is the most direct test for the shortest fully resolved method. Holding phi0, phi1, and T constant isolates slope effects on the critical pair.

At 14 min the critical pair lost resolution, while 16 min was fully resolved but slightly too slow; raising temperature may pull the last peak under 10 min while modestly changing selectivity enough to preserve or improve the 6/7 separation. This directly tests whether temperature can beat the current best without sacrificing full resolution.

The 6/7 pair is highly temperature-sensitive and worsened at 45 C, so test the opposite direction at the known safe 16 min slope. Lower temperature may improve that selectivity enough to keep full resolution while increasing retention only modestly, potentially leaving CRF near or above the current best.

Temperature changes hurt selectivity, so return to 40 C and test whether a slightly shallower gradient restores full resolution while keeping the last peak close to 10 min. This brackets the optimum between 16 and 20 min and may outperform both by giving all pairs >=1.5 with a smaller time penalty than 20 min.

The peaks elute over a relatively narrow effective solvent window, so trimming the gradient range should reduce the time spent at unnecessarily strong conditions while keeping the same slope neighborhood. This tests whether a tighter phi window can keep full resolution and pull the last peak below 10 min without relying on temperature shifts that damaged selectivity.

A narrower window at 16 min preserved full resolution but was too slow, while 14 min with the broad window was fast but failed on the 6/7 pair. This intermediate window/slope combination may keep the late peak under 10 min while giving the critical middle pair just enough extra separation.

The current best is very close to ideal but still misses full credit on the 6/7 pair, so make the gradient one step shallower while keeping the promising narrowed window. This should nudge that pair above R = 1.5, and if t_last stays near 10 min it could reach or beat the current best.

At 14 min, phi1 = 0.90 nearly achieved perfect resolution with no time penalty; a small increase in phi1 may pull the last peak slightly earlier while preserving or modestly improving the 6/7 selectivity within the same fast gradient. This is a focused refinement around the current best region rather than changing temperature, which proved risky.

The best run so far is just shy of full credit on the 6/7 pair, and raising phi1 worsened that pair, so test the complementary direction by lowering phi0 while keeping the successful 14 min, phi1 0.90 framework. This may shift the critical middle selectivity enough to push R above 1.5 while still keeping the last peak under 10 min.

The 14 min, phi1 0.90 region is best, and lowering phi0 improved neither time nor the critical pair enough, so now test the other side of the window. Raising phi0 may selectively decompress the mid-gradient cluster around peaks 5–8 while keeping the run under 10 min.

Around 14 min, phi1 = 0.90 gave the best balance, but the critical pair still sits just below 1.5; slightly lowering phi1 may reduce gradient steepness enough to improve that pair without pushing t_last past 10 min. This is a targeted one-step refinement within the best-performing region.

We have reached the maximum CRF, so the remaining useful task is to see whether an even shorter method can keep all pairs at or above 1.5 and t_last within 10 min. Shortening tG by one step directly tests whether injection 13 is the shortest fully resolved method or if there is a faster tie.

The 14 min, 0.10–0.85 window is optimal at 40 C, but t_last sits right at the 10 min limit; a modest temperature increase could create a faster tied optimum if the critical 6/7 pair remains above 1.5. This is worth one direct check now that the maximum score has been reached.

Since the winning method is only barely at the 10 min limit, try a slightly higher phi0 with the same optimal phi1 and tG to see if the last peak moves earlier while maintaining the now-validated selectivity zone. This is a focused tie-seeking variant around the proven optimum without the severe selectivity penalty seen from temperature changes.

Injection 16 improved the fully resolved tied optimum by bringing the last peak earlier, so continue in the same direction with one more phi0 step while holding phi1 and tG fixed. This tests whether we can keep all pairs above 1.5 and obtain an even shorter best-in-class tied method.

Raising phi0 further hurt the critical 6/7 pair, so keep the successful phi0 = 0.15 and instead lower phi1 one step to slightly flatten the gradient while staying in the same fast window. This may preserve full resolution and pull more of the separation into the gradient, potentially giving another tied optimum with similar or better runtime.

We already have tied-optimal methods, so now probe whether a higher temperature can be compensated by a shallower gradient in the best phi window to create a faster or equally good alternative. This isolates whether the severe 45 C selectivity loss can be rescued by reduced slope around the proven 0.15–0.85 window.

Temperature increases consistently destroyed the key 6/7 selectivity, so check the opposite direction in the best window to complete the temperature map around the tied-optimal method. A lower temperature might strengthen that already acceptable pair enough to identify the most robust fully resolved condition, even if it is not faster.

Both 0.10–0.85 and 0.15–0.80 regions bracket full-resolution performance, so test the combined lower-window corner to complete the local map around the tied optima. This checks whether a slightly flatter gradient centered a bit earlier can retain full resolution while moving the last peak below both current tied bests.

The maximum score is already secured, so use remaining budget to probe for a very fast alternative at higher temperature and shorter gradient in the best phi window. Even though 45 C hurt selectivity before, combining it with a shorter method maps an extreme edge of the design space and confirms whether any hidden faster tie exists.

The 12 min method at 40 C was close but under-resolved on 6/7, and lower temperature shifted the critical selectivity toward earlier pairs rather than 6/7 in the 14 min run. Testing 12 min at 35 C checks the last untried route to a shorter fully resolved method in the best solvent window.

With only two injections left and the optimum already achieved, explore the remaining untested phi0 side at the winning phi1/tG/T to fully map robustness of the best solvent window. This checks whether lowering phi0 from 0.10 or 0.15 can still preserve full resolution while offering any useful selectivity margin insight around the critical pair.

For the final injection, probe the last untested phi1 side around the tied-optimal phi0 = 0.15, tG = 14, T = 40 condition. This completes the local window map and confirms whether stronger final eluent can preserve full resolution while shifting the run later or earlier relative to the best method.
